alignment.note: Greek ἀπῆλθον ('they went away') is rendered by the Peshitta with the single verb ܘܐܙܠܘ, which also carries the conjunction. The Vulgate expands the action into a participle of embarking (ascendentes, 'going up [into the boat]') plus the main verb abierunt, splitting one Greek aorist into two coordinated Latin verbal elements.

Greek and Latin both employ a prepositional phrase with the article/no-article for 'in the boat' (ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ / in navim), the Vulgate's accusative reflecting the motion-of-embarking idiom; the Peshitta uses a single proclitic-prefixed noun ܒܣܦܝܢܬܐ ('by/in [the] ship'), placing it after the destination rather than before, a difference of word order.

Greek εἰς ἔρημον τόπον and Latin in desertum locum agree in adjective-noun order ('into a deserted place'); the Peshitta inverts to noun-then-attribute ܠܐܬܪܐ ܚܘܪܒܐ ('to a place, a desolate one'), the normal Syriac construct/attributive sequence.

The Greek idiom κατ᾽ ἰδίαν ('privately, by themselves') is a two-word prepositional adverbial; the Vulgate compresses it to the single adverb seorsum, while the Peshitta uses the suffixed reflexive ܒܠܚܘܕܝܗܘܢ ('by themselves'), explicitly marking the third-plural subject that the Greek and Latin leave implicit.
